Senses.Explanation: In the Chan records the ordinary monastic water-vessel is repurposed as a naming-and-checking test-object: the master forbids calling the bottle by its own name and demands a different response, and knocking it over settles a succession contest. In the Baizhang–Guishan encounter Baizhang points to the bottle and asks what it should be called if it may not be called a clean-water bottle (不得喚作淨瓶); the head cook Guishan answers not in words but by knocking it over (蹋倒淨瓶), and is thereby recorded as the successor. That test-object deployment — who sets the test and what the kick decides — is the word's Zen bend. Literally a ‘clean bottle,’ this is a bottle used for water. The allowlisted corpus has 487 hits in 143 texts. Recorded actions establish the object without requiring an imported technical gloss: a teacher asks for the bottle to be passed and then returned to its former place; another calls an attendant and says, ‘Add water to the clean-water bottle’; Guishan passes one to Yangshan and draws it back before Yangshan can receive it; and one biography reports water surging from a bottle. It is also the object in the Baizhang–Guishan case: Baizhang points to it and asks what it should be called if it may not be called a clean-water bottle, after which Guishan knocks it over. Later collections title and repeatedly comment on this case. The word continues to name the concrete bottle throughout those exchanges.
Senses.Note: The Zen bend is institutional, not a separate lexical sense: the ordinary water-vessel becomes the naming-test object whose knocking-over decides a succession (不得喚作淨瓶 … 蹋倒淨瓶). The seven required definition formulas were searched. The corpus does not supply a separate lexical equation, but it repeatedly identifies the object through passing, filling, returning, tipping, and knocking it over. The failed draft candidate from the Tianyin record was excluded because its proposed span did not pass exact verification; no unverified text was retained.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Baizhang–Guishan succession encounter records Baizhang pointing to the bottle, Hualin answering, and Guishan knocking it over.

Senses.Explanation: A reduplicated descriptive phrase: clean or clear (淨) and bare (裸裸), hence "clean and bare." It occurs 326 times in 127 allowlisted texts. The corpus supplies its own unpacking: "clean and bare, with nothing left; red and free, wholly exposed" (淨裸裸無遺，赤灑灑全露). It repeatedly joins the paired phrase "red and free" (赤灑灑): 54 occurrences with the graph 'sprinkle' (灑) and 12 with its variant graph 'sprinkle' (洒). Other predicates keep the description concrete: "the sand-world is clean and bare" (沙界淨裸裸), "clean and bare, with nothing to grasp" (淨裸裸，沒可把), and "clean and bare, red and free; still resembling an ordinary person as before" (淨裸裸赤灑灑，依前似平常人). The phrase describes what a passage presents as exposed, unleft-over, or ungraspable.
Senses.Note: The adverbial form "cleanly bare" (淨裸裸地) occurs 15 times in eight texts. Records also make the full paired phrase the condition in a direct question: "when clean and bare, red and free, how do you conduct yourself?" (淨裸裸赤洒洒時，作麼生行履). This question shows that the description is not treated as a final interpretive label. The alternate spelling "red and free" (赤洒洒) is preserved where it occurs; translations do not silently regularize the source graphs.

Occurrences.Kwic: 機輪未轉。大地黑漫漫。古鏡當軒。沙界淨裸裸。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Parallel descriptions: before the mechanism turns, the earth is black and boundless; when the ancient mirror faces the hall, the sand-world is clean and bare.

Occurrences.Kwic: 淨裸裸無遺。赤灑灑全露。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Compact internal paraphrase: clean and bare, with nothing left; red and free, wholly exposed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 淨裸裸赤灑灑。依前似平常人。由爾有事也得。無事也得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The paired description is followed by still resembling an ordinary person as before; having affairs or having none are both permitted.
The paired variant spelling is immediately predicated as having nothing to grasp.

Occurrences.Kwic: 小參僧問。淨裸裸赤洒洒時。作麼生行履。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct question: when clean and bare, red and free, how does one conduct oneself?

Senses.PreferredTarget: polishing a tile to make a mirror
AlternateTargets: grinding a brick into a mirror
polish a tile and make a mirror
Senses.Explanation: Literally, polishing or grinding (磨) a tile or brick (磚) to make (作) a mirror (鏡): "polishing a tile to make a mirror." This graph form occurs 43 times in 37 allowlisted texts. Graphic variants include "polishing a tile to make a mirror" (磨甎作鏡, 19 hits in 13 texts) and the form with another tile graph (磨塼作鏡, 5 in 5); "polishing a tile into a mirror" (磨磚成鏡) occurs 8 times in 5. In the defining encounter, Mazu Daoyi is sitting Chan to become a buddha. Nan'yue Huairang polishes a tile; asked why, he says he is making a mirror. Mazu says, "how could polishing a tile make a mirror?" Huairang answers, "if polishing a tile cannot make a mirror, how could your sitting Chan make a buddha?" (磨甎既不成鏡，汝坐禪豈得成佛). The exchange continues with the comparison of a cart that will not move: should one strike the cart or the ox? Later records use the compact phrase as the name of this encounter and as an explicit comparison for futile effort: Huanglong pairs "searching the sea and counting sand, vainly spending strength" with "polishing a tile to make a mirror, uselessly applying effort" (入海算沙，空自費力；磨塼作鏡，枉用功夫). Fachang compares private explanations and forced elaboration to it. Songgu compilations preserve named comments that call "sitting Chan to become a buddha" a sickness in the heart and "making a mirror by polishing a tile" a flower before the eyes. Zen therefore bends an impossible craft operation into the roster-name of Huairang's encounter with Mazu and a corpus-attested comparison for wasted construction; its application to sitting Chan is spoken by Huairang inside the case, not supplied by this entry.
Senses.Note: The graph for "tile" alternates among the standard form (磚) and two graphic variants (甎 and 塼) across witnesses. The first graphic variant (甎) appears in important early lamp and case-compilation witnesses. This entry groups those orthographic variants but does not count them toward the exact 43-hit headword total.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師曰：磨甎作什麼？讓曰：磨甎作鏡。師曰：磨甎豈得成鏡？讓曰：磨甎既不成鏡，汝坐禪豈得成佛？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Continued Lamp Record preserves the defining Huairang-Mazu exchange: the impossible mirror is directly compared with sitting Chan to become a buddha.

Occurrences.Kwic: 磨磚作鏡、打車打牛，小兒子戲；黃檗喫棒、大愚還拳，小兒子戲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shending Yikui groups polishing the tile and striking cart or ox together as children's play, showing the compact phrase functioning as the name of the case.

Senses.Explanation: The named shout associated by the Chan record with Linji Yixuan. Device lists pair 'Linji's shout' with 'Deshan's staff,' and later sermons compare the shout to rushing thunder. The phrase is not merely a historical label: masters publicly ask what its purport is, demand that a monk produce it, or declare that they have no use for it today. The corpus also polices the inherited emblem. When asked what indication lies beyond Deshan's staff and Linji's shout, one master strikes and says that calling it 'staff-and-shout' sends one to hell like an arrow. Thus Zen bends an ordinary shout into a named lineage implement and object of later interview, imitation, comparison, and criticism; the entry reports only those recorded deployments.
Senses.Note: Wave-plan frequency: 410; related-entry counts report roughly 442 hits in 155 allowlist texts. Family comparison with the shout (喝), the staff or blow (棒), Deshan's staff (德山棒), and staff-and-shout (棒喝) confirms a genuinely Linji-specific named phrase, hence MasterName is set. The physical vocal act and the inherited label refer to the same named shout, not two things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟喝，德山棒，留與禪人作模範
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A device list explicitly pairs Linji's shout with Deshan's staff and calls them models left to Chan people.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德山棒如雨點。臨濟喝似雷奔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's record carries the stock similes: Deshan's staff like raindrops and Linji's shout like rushing thunder.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問德山棒臨濟喝意旨如何師云寶應今日不用
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question asks the purport of the paired devices; the master says Baoying has no use for them today.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：「德山棒、臨濟喝，除此二途，有何指示？」師打云：「喚作棒喝，入地獄如箭。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked for an indication beyond the two devices, the master strikes and warns against naming the action 'staff-and-shout.'
